title: 3 Impact of N Fertilization and Inoculation on Nutritive Value and Nitrate Levels of Sorghum-Sudangrass Baleage
content:
Abstract
The objective of this study is to evaluate the effect of increased N fertilization rates on NO3 ̄ concentration and nutritive value of sorghum-sudangrass and measure the changes following an ensiling period with and without bacterial inoculant. Sorghum-sudangrass (Sorghum x drummondii), a warm season annual forage, provides farmers in temperate and warm regions with high yielding, quick growing, and nutrient dense forage during the summer months, extending the grazing season. Although by nature a hardy forage, able to withstand stressful drought periods, environmental stressors can create an accumulation of nitrates (NO3 ̄), especially with additional fertilization (Hancock et al., 2018). NO3 ̄ concentration above 2,500 ppm in ruminant feeds can increase the risk of nitrate poisoning – leading to decreased milk production, reduced weight gain, a lower immune system, abortions, and death (Strickland et al., 2017). Studies have shown potential for a NO3 ̄ degradation effect following fermentation through ensiling in contrast to conventional hay production (Bai et al., 2022). In part I of this study, fifteen ‘Greengrazer’ sorghum-sudangrass plots were planted in May 2024 with N fertilization rate treatments of 0, 50, 100, 151, and 202 kg N/ha (conducted in triplicate). In August, harvested samples were weighed and analyzed for herbage mass and nutritive value. NIRS analyses showed the greatest nutritive variation in crude protein (CP) concentration as fertilization rates increased, resulting in, on average, 7.8, 9.0, 11.3, 15.8, and 16.7% CP, respectively for each treatment rate. Similarly, herbage mass increased with treatment rate, showing, on average, 5,021, 5,577, 6,874, 8,151, and 7,686 kg/ha, respectively. Wet chemistry triplicate data was used to determine NO3 ̄ concentration, revealing 151 and 202 kg N/ha resulting in 7,429 and 11,494 NO3 ̄ ppm, respectively, values outside the safe threshold when feeding ruminant livestock. In part II of this study, six samples from five groups of forage with varying nitrate levels were wilted to 55% moisture. Half were inoculated with Promote® Forage-Mate® EBL, and all samples were placed into vacuum-sealed bags for a 6-week ensiling period. All samples from each treatment group showed a decrease in NO3 ̄ concentration, ranging from 10%-53%. Inoculation resulted in a higher NO3 ̄ decrease in groups with lower initial NO3 ̄ ppm but a lower NO3 ̄ degradation percent in groups with higher initial NO3 ̄ concentrations. Ensiling with or without inoculant was unable to decrease samples with unsafe NO3 ̄ levels below the recommended feeding threshold. This initial year of data supports the increase in nutritive value with applied N fertilizer but also NO3 ̄ concentration that can be harmful to livestock as well as NO3 ̄ degradation potential with ensiling with little impact from inoculation.
